title: Blackbox regression drilldown - INT8 / AWQ / FP8 + KV cache pathology
summary: Deep technical investigation into a recent accuracy regression observed after rolling AWQ/INT8 mixed precision onto Polaris' on-prem cluster. Discussed KV cache staleness interactions with quantized KV layout, layerwise sensitivity hypotheses, fallback strategies, and an on-prem stress benchmark plan.
topics: INT8 vs AWQ vs FP8 accuracy tradeoffs
KV cache staleness and sticky batch interactions
On-prem benchmarking plan and data/telemetry to collect
next_steps: Omar to run layerwise sensitivity sweep (per-layer MSE & accuracy) and upload CSV to shared folder by 2026-07-21
Raj to provision a 4-node on-prem test slice with KV cache instrumentation and provide access creds by 2026-07-20
Maya to send security docs and the AWQ reproducibility checklist
Schedule follow-up triage on 2026-07-23 at 16:00 UTC to review sweep results and agree rollback policy
action_items: Omar - run layerwise quantize-and-eval (INT8/AWQ/FP8) on model 'polaris-gpt-13b' and share results (due 2026-07-21)
Raj - enable detailed KV cache telemetry (hits, stale evictions, per-shard lag) and share logs (due 2026-07-20)
Maya - send AWQ tuning guide and internal regression playbook link (due 2026-07-16)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. we scheduled 50 minutes to go through the regression you saw after the AWQ rollout.
[00:00:10] Raj (Customer): yeah thanks Maya, uh quick background — we flipped AWQ+int8 on last tuesday on our 4-node onprem cluster, we were seeing a 1.8% drop on our intent classification suite, mostly in longer prompts. latency was fine but accuracy dip is what triggered this.
[00:00:28] Lina (SRE): and we started seeing more 5xx fallbacks when kv looked stale, it felt correlated, not sure yet.
[00:00:35] Omar (Redwood SE): okay good context. can you remind us which model variant you rolled, and whether you used per-channel scales or symmetric quant?
[00:00:44] Raj: it's polaris-gpt-13b, we used the AWQ recipe from last month, default per-channel for weights, asymmetric activations, and a hybrid approach where we kept first 6 layers in fp16.
[00:00:55] Omar: interesting — first question: were positional embs or rotary params changed? sometimes rotary mixing with AWQ's quant noise shows up for longer sequences.
[00:01:02] Raj: no changes to rotary. sequence lengths do go up to 2k in some pipelines.
[00:01:08] Omar: okay. let's walk through what folks observed — Lina, you said 5xxs?
[00:01:13] Lina: yeah, intermittent 500 on a few requests; trace showed the runtime tried to fetch kv from the local cache, but the cached entry was stale and then we had to do a remote fetch which timed out under tail load. seemed to cluster around heavy batching moments.
[00:01:28] Maya: that suggests a KV cache staleness interaction with batching. one thing we've seen is that when KV buffers are quantized in memory layout changes, the cache hit spec changes slightly, which can exacerbate sticky batching artifacts.
[00:01:41] Raj: sticky batching? like the old requests keep their kv stuck?
[00:01:45] Omar: yeah, by sticky batching I mean when runtime groups requests with similar prefixes to maximize cache reuse; if quantized KV keys collide or align differently under AWQ, you can get more coherent misses. also we should consider alignment/padding differences for int8 layouts — it changes the address offsets.
[00:01:59] Lina: that could explain why it manifests under heavy batching, because the runtime pushes aggressive coalescing.
[00:02:05] Raj: ok, so is this more of a correctness/accuracy issue or a perf issue causing timeouts which then cascade to poor responses?
[00:02:13] Omar: both. the accuracy delta you reported (1.8%) could be from quant noise in certain layers (we need per-layer numbers), and the perf/timeouts make it worse by dropping state occasionally. when KV misses occur it forces model to recompute states which with quantization can diverge.
[00:02:28] Maya: quick sanity check — did you have any fallback policy enabled? e.g. runtime fallback to fp16 when confidence drops?
[00:02:33] Raj: we did not enable automatic fp16 fallback, we just switched model binary.
[00:02:37] Omar: ok that's a lever we can recommend. runtime gating: detect per-token quality score and if it crosses threshold, route to fp16 variant for that request.
[00:02:46] [00:02:46] Speaker 6: (murmur)
[00:02:50] Raj: can that be toggled without redeploying?
[00:02:53] Omar: yes, on Redwood Dedicated and Private you can enable a runtime flag for precision fallbacks; it has a small throughput cost but preserves tail accuracy.
[00:03:01] Lina: good to know.
[00:03:04] Maya: let's capture hypotheses. Omar, do you want to list possible root causes?
[00:03:08] Omar: sure — 1) layerwise sensitivity: some middle layers (6-10) may be sensitive; 2) kv layout/addressing change under AWQ/int8 causing higher collision/miss rate; 3) longer sequences amplifying rotary/relative pos quant noise; 4) sticky batching magnifying rare misses into systemic errors.
[00:03:26] Raj: which of these would cause accuracy drop and not just perf?
[00:03:30] Omar: the layerwise sensitivity is the primary candidate for accuracy. int8/AWQ doesn't treat all layers equally — transformer attention matrices often need higher precision in certain layers. AWQ's stochastic rounding can also shift logits slightly leading to different argmaxes for some classes.
[00:03:46] Raj: we did an initial quick A/B but I admit it was coarse.
[00:03:49] Lina: question — FP8 is something we considered. would moving to FP8 fix this or make it worse?
[00:03:55] Omar: FP8 can help for layers that require dynamic range — it often reduces absolute error vs int8 for activations, but it's hardware dependent. on your A100 onprem boxes FP8 path is experimental in our runtime and gains are nuanced; might help but would need careful calibration.
[00:04:10] Maya: also cost tradeoff — FP8 can increase memory slightly or require different kernels which may reduce throughput.
[00:04:16] Raj: can we talk about AWQ vs GPTQ? we used AWQ because internal bench looked best previously.
[00:04:22] Omar: AWQ tends to be faster to apply and gives good compression with per-channel quant, GPTQ can often yield better accuracy because it does second-order layerwise calibration but it's slower to compute. AWQ can be tuned (layer skip, clamp params), GPTQ might be the fallback if AWQ can't regain accuracy.
[00:04:38] Lina: and AWQ interacts with KV cache how?
[00:04:41] Omar: the in-memory layout for KV under AWQ uses packed int8 blocks and a small scale table; if the cache keying hashes on the raw serialized bytes, small differences in packing order can change the cache key leading to misses.
[00:04:55] Raj: that seems bad — can we canonicalize keys before cache?
[00:04:58] Omar: yes we can — one mitigation is to use logical keys derived from token indices + model version rather than raw bytes; that avoids packing-induced misses. it's a config change but worth doing.
[00:05:07] Maya: what telemetry would prove this?
[00:05:10] Omar: per-key miss histogram, pre- and post-pack checksum comparison, and a delta on miss rates correlated with batch size. Raj, can you enable per-key checksums in your KV trace?
[00:05:20] Raj: will do. I'll enable both checksum and raw byte dump for a sample period.
[00:05:23] [00:05:23] Speaker 6: (typing)
[00:05:27] Lina: on the runtime side we also saw small increases in tail latency at 95th pct — from 210ms to ~290ms during heavy batching.
[00:05:34] Omar: that aligns with remote fetch fallback. if your KV misses and you do a remote fetch under load, tail latency spikes which can push requests into error.
[00:05:41] Raj: so immediate mitigations? what can we toggle to stop the customer-visible regression?
[00:05:45] Omar: short-term: 1) enable precision fallback for tail cases (route to fp16) 2) reduce aggressive coalescing/batching thresholds to lower sticky batching 3) canonicalize KV keys to avoid pack-based cache misses.
[00:05:58] Maya: and medium-term: run a layerwise sensitivity sweep to identify sensitive layers to keep at fp16 in mixed precision.
[00:06:05] Raj: Omar, you mentioned per-layer sweep. what's the exact experiment?
[00:06:09] Omar: we'll quantize the model under three recipes (INT8 baseline, AWQ tuned, FP8 experimental) and then iteratively keep individual layers at fp16 while quantizing the rest. We'll evaluate on your regression prompt set and compute per-layer delta in accuracy and token-level MSE.
[00:06:25] Raj: how long will that take?
[00:06:27] Omar: with your dataset and our GPU seats we estimate ~24-36 hours for a full sweep. we'll prioritize the middle layers first.
[00:06:33] Raj: fine.
[00:06:35] Lina: any concerns about our VPC/onprem networking causing false positives? we run internal NAT and the nodes can see each other, but sometimes the NICs drop packets under burst load.
[00:06:44] Omar: that's possible. telemetry from your network stack + runtime traces will help. the more data we have, the faster we can correlate.
[00:06:50] Maya: let's also discuss rollback strategy — if the sweep finds layer 8 is the culprit, what's minimal rollback?
[00:06:56] Omar: minimal rollback: pin that layer to fp16 and rebuild a mixed-precision binary, then canary that version on 5% of traffic. our rollout system supports per-layer pinning without redeploying the entire model across all nodes; it's a small build but quick to roll.
[00:07:10] Raj: per-layer pinning without full redeploy? sounds great. any perf hit?
[00:07:14] Omar: small, depends on how many layers you pin; one or two layers typically hits throughput by ~2-5% but reclaim accuracy.
[00:07:20] Lina: we need that tradeoff chart.
[00:07:22] Maya: Omar will include perf delta table in the sweep artifact.
[00:07:26] Omar: yes — I'll include throughput/latency/accuracy for each config.
[00:07:29] Raj: about data: should we run the sweep on masked production traces or a sanitized eval set?
[00:07:35] Omar: a mix. start with sanitized eval for reproducibility, then replay a small production trace in a test slice to confirm behavior under realistic prefixes.
[00:07:44] Raj: ok.
[00:07:46] Lina: one more question — we saw divergence in certain user intents only; could training-time tokenization differences with quantization explain that?
[00:07:55] Omar: tokenization differences usually affect embedding stage; quantization mostly affects linear ops. but combined they can push logits across decision boundaries. we'll check token distribution for the failing intents.
[00:08:04] Maya: let's capture the immediate tasks again — Omar runs the sweep, Raj enables KV telemetry and provides access, Maya sends playbook and schedules follow-up.
[00:08:12] Raj: I'll have logs and a sample raw dump by Monday.
[00:08:16] Omar: also one low-friction change: canonicalize cache keys to logical IDs instead of byte-serialized stacks; we can ship that as a config and it should reduce pack related misses.
[00:08:26] Raj: please send the config diff.
[00:08:28] Maya: will do.
[00:08:31] [00:08:31] Speaker 6: (background noise)
[00:08:36] Raj: any other gotchas we should watch for?
[00:08:39] Omar: watch for staleness windows — KV eviction TTLs that are too short can make the problem worse under bursty traffic. also check shard imbalance.
[00:08:47] Lina: good note. we'll audit TTLs.
[00:08:50] Maya: timeline — Omar delivers sweep artifacts by 2026-07-21, follow-up triage 2026-07-23. Raj delivers telemetry by 2026-07-20.
[00:08:59] Raj: sounds good. thanks Omar and Maya.
[00:09:03] Omar: thanks everyone. one last thing — I'll include a recommended canary policy and example metric thresholds (accuracy delta > 0.5% => rollback, kv-miss-rate > 0.2% => block AWQ rollout).
[00:09:16] Lina: excellent.
[00:09:18] Maya: ok wrapping up — I'll email notes and links to the sweep doc and the KV telemetry config.
[00:09:24] Raj: thanks.
[00:09:26] [00:09:26] End of call
